sources.excerpt: Jam Pedals Rattler MKII: The Boutique Classic Just Got An Upgrade! For a better experience on Gearnews, we recommend JavaScript to be enabled. Home Guitar Synths Studio Drums Live Tech Other Deals LinkedIn Instagram Facebook Twitter RSS EN DE EN ES FR IT About us Privacy Policy Imprint Contact Cookie Settings gearnews Guitar Synths Studio Drums Live Tech Other Deals Search LinkedIn Instagram Facebook Twitter RSS Search EN DE EN ES FR IT Jam Pedals Rattler MKII: The Boutique Classic Just Got An Upgrade! The Rattler MKII brings exciting new functionality and tonal abilities to the classic Rat circuit! 19 Jul 2024   by   Cole  | |     | 5,0 / 5,0 |   Reading time: 2 min Jam Rattler MKII  ·  Source: Jam Pedals Previous Next ADVERTISEMENT A new update to the Jam Pedals Rattler brings welcome changes and extended functionality to both the guitar and bass versions of the ProCo Rat-based distortion pedal. ADVERTISEMENT What’s New With The Rattler MKII For Jam’s second reimagining of the legendary ProCo Rat distortion pedal, they’ve added some extra features not typically found on other iterations of pedals based on this same topology. A second footswitch engages a standalone mid-boost, providing enhanced tonal options. The custom op-amp emulates the sound and feel of the original LM308 chip, ensuring a classic distortion experience. The clipping toggle switch allows you to select between asymmetrical (like the original) or symmetrical clipping, offering greater versatility. The click-less footswitch uses relays for a soft touch on/off operation, enhancing usability. Additionally, the selectable start-up state feature lets you choose whether the pedal is on or off by default when power is applied, giving you more control over your setup. The Rattler MKII On Bass For bass players, Jam is offering this pedal with an inverted color scheme, but don’t be fooled. The Bass Rattler MKII has some extra tricks up its sleeve that make it a flexible tool for adding distortion to lower frequencies. ADVERTISEMENT The pedal features a wet/dry blend or “Mix” control to retain clarity and articulation, even with heavy distortion. A second footswitch engages a higher gain stage for quick moments of heavy saturation. The Bass Rattler MKII also offers higher headroom than its guitar counterpart, making it ideal for bass players seeking versatile distortion options. The new Jam Pedals Rattler MKII is available now at Thomann* for $218.00 / £202.00 / 239.00€ and $209.00 / £194.00 / 229.00€ for the bass version. But with the LM308 chip used in the original Rat and Rattler pedal, sometimes "New Old Stock" becomes "No Old Stock". Enter the new JAM Rattler MkII. For the new Rattler, JAM develop their own discrete component analog Op Amp to replace the LM308. Discrete components means that it's constructed of individual components (resistors, transistors, etc.) rather than a miniaturized integrated circuit (the "chip" seen on the circuit board of many effect pedals). Looking inside you'll notice that the new JAM circuit is a good bit larger than the typical chip (see photos). While they had the hood open, JAM also added a midrange boost footswitch, and a toggle to select symmetrical or asymmetrical clipping (the original Rattler is asymmetrical-only, while the Rattler LTD is symmetrical). So how does it sound?  The new MkII Rattler retains what we love about the original: Incredibly tasty grind that thickens single notes like few other pedals can, without becoming compressed and mushy. In asymmetrical form you get the true "Rat" tone which can take you from light overdrive to aggressive distortion/fuzz. The symmetrical mode is a little smoother and thicker sounding, and a touch less "nasty". Your preference may depend on your amp, pickups, etc. With a Strat or P-90 we were digging the symmetrical, while humbuckers may benefit from the extra edge of asymmetrical.  The mid-boost footswitch is internally adjustable for boost level and bass content, and as JAM says, it's not a volume boost. It's big, thick, meaty and makes the Rattler a true two-function pedal. It's a whole new dimension of Rattler, and definitely benefits from the added functionality of the internal trimmers.  Differences? The natural voicing seems a little warmer than the original, and we like the way it works with single coils. With the old Rattler we typically had the tone around 9 o'clock, and with the MkII there is more usable range. However, the hallmark of the original LM308 Rattler is how it cleans up on turn-down.
